nameStory: The One-armed Jelly gets its quirky name from its distinctive single, long tentacle that dangles below like a lonely arm reaching into the water. Unlike most jellies that have multiple tentacles arranged in a circle, this hydrozoan looks like it's waving hello with just one appendage!
description: The One-armed Jelly is actually a colonial hydrozoan, not a true jellyfish, that lives attached to hard surfaces on the seafloor. It consists of a slender, stalk-like body topped with a bulbous head ringed by short feeding tentacles, plus that signature single long trailing tentacle below. The whole organism can reach 4-6 inches tall, with the long tentacle extending even further when fully stretched.

idTips.label: Single long tentacle
idTips.description: One distinctive trailing tentacle hangs down like a fishing line, often extending 2-3 times the length of the main body and swaying gently with the current

idTips.label: Bulbous head
idTips.description: The top forms a rounded, swollen structure that looks almost like a tiny light bulb, semi-transparent with a pinkish or yellowish tint

idTips.label: Slender stalk
idTips.description: The main body is a thin, flexible column that bends and sways with water movement, feeling soft and gelatinous if gently touched

idTips.label: Crown of short tentacles
idTips.description: Around the bulbous head, numerous short tentacles wave like tiny fingers, creating a feathery appearance when feeding

idTips.label: Attached base
idTips.description: Always found firmly anchored to rocks, shells, or other hard surfaces - never free-swimming like true jellies

habitat: Found in deeper coastal waters of New England, typically 30-200 feet down, attached to rocky bottoms, shipwrecks, or large shells. Most commonly encountered by scuba divers or brought up in fishing nets or lobster traps from these deeper, cooler waters.

seasonality.spring: Begins growing from overwintered base structures. Young colonies start small and may be easily overlooked during this season.
seasonality.summer: Reaches full size and reproductive maturity. This is when the characteristic long tentacle is most fully developed and visible.
seasonality.fall: Still actively feeding and reproducing. Colonies remain at peak size and are most likely to be noticed by divers or fishermen.
seasonality.winter: Many colonies die back to basal structures, though some may persist in deeper, more stable waters throughout the cold months.

funFact: **Uncertainty flag**: The One-armed Jelly can actually regenerate its entire body from just a small piece of its base - if the colony gets damaged by storms or predators, it can regrow its distinctive bulbous head and trailing tentacle within weeks, like an underwater phoenix rising from the ashes!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with small sea anemones when the long tentacle is retracted, but anemones have their tentacles arranged in a flat circle on top, while this species has its feeding tentacles around a bulbous head on a stalk. Remember: anemones are like underwater flowers, one-armed jellies are like underwater lollipops with a string attached.
contextualKnowledge: Despite its common name, this isn't actually a jellyfish at all - it's a hydrozoan, which is a colonial animal more closely related to corals and sea anemones. The confusion comes from its gelatinous, translucent appearance, but unlike true jellies, it spends its life anchored in one spot.
compareHints: **Uncertainty flag**: Since no other Corymorpha species are recorded in New England waters, compare with other colonial hydrozoans like Tubularia. One-armed Jellies are distinguished by having just one long tentacle versus Tubularia's multiple tentacles of similar length, and by their more pronounced bulbous head structure.
